claim: IFT is essential for the elongation and maintenance of eukaryotic cilia and flagella.
source: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) is essential for the elongation and maintenance of eukaryotic cilia and flagella.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Anterograde trains split apart at the ciliary tip.
source: Anterograde trains split apart and IFT complexes mix with each other at the tip to assemble retrograde trains.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the PhotoGate experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: IFT complexes mix with each other at the tip to assemble retrograde trains.
source: Anterograde trains split apart and IFT complexes mix with each other at the tip to assemble retrograde trains.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the PhotoGate experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Dynein-1b is carried to the tip by kinesin-II as inactive cargo on anterograde trains.
source: Dynein-1b is carried to the tip by kinesin-II as inactive cargo on anterograde trains.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the two-color imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Kinesin-II detaches from IFT trains at the tip and diffuses in flagella.
source: Unlike dynein-1b, kinesin-II detaches from IFT trains at the tip and diffuses in flagella.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the PhotoGate experiments tracking KAP-GFP described in the manuscript.

claim: As the flagellum grows longer, diffusion delays return of kinesin-II to the basal body.
source: As the flagellum grows longer, diffusion delays return of kinesin-II to the basal body, depleting kinesin-II available for anterograde transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diffusion measurements and modeling described in the manuscript.

claim: Diffusion of kinesin-II depletes kinesin-II available for anterograde transport.
source: As the flagellum grows longer, diffusion delays return of kinesin-II to the basal body, depleting kinesin-II available for anterograde transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the confocal microscopy measurements during flagellar regrowth.

claim: Dissociation of kinesin-II from IFT trains serves as a negative feedback mechanism that facilitates flagellar length control in Chlamydomonas.
source: Our results suggest that dissociation of kinesin-II from IFT trains serves as a negative feedback mechanism that facilitates flagellar length control in Chlamydomonas.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript based on multiple experimental observations and modeling.

claim: Cilia are hair-like organelles that extend from the plasma membrane of nearly all mammalian cells.
source: Cilia (or eukaryotic flagella, terms essentially referring to the same organelle) are hair-like organelles that extend from the plasma membrane of nearly all mammalian cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field cited in the introduction.

claim: The core structural component of a cilium is the axoneme.
source: The core structural component of a cilium is the axoneme, a ring of nine unipolar doublet microtubules surrounding a central pair of singlet microtubules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ciliary structure.

claim: The axoneme is a ring of nine unipolar doublet microtubules surrounding a central pair of singlet microtubules.
source: The core structural component of a cilium is the axoneme, a ring of nine unipolar doublet microtubules surrounding a central pair of singlet microtubules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axoneme structure.

claim: Cilia play essential roles in cell motility, generate the movement of fluids over multiciliated surfaces, and sense extracellular signals.
source: Cilia play essential roles in cell motility, generate the movement of fluids over multiciliated surfaces, and sense extracellular signals (Satir et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The IFT machinery transports axonemal precursors and sensory proteins bidirectionally between the cell body and the ciliary tip.
source: To assemble and maintain functional cilia, the IFT machinery (Kozminski et al., 1993) transports axonemal precursors and sensory proteins bidirectionally between the cell body and the ciliary tip.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Defects in IFT are linked to a wide range of human diseases including Bardet-Biedl syndrome, retinal degeneration, and polycystic kidney disease.
source: Defects in IFT are linked to a wide range of human diseases including Bardet-Biedl syndrome, retinal degeneration, and polycystic kidney disease (Brown and Witman, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Intraflagellar cargoes interact with multiprotein complexes known as IFT particles that are organized into larger IFT trains as they enter the flagellum.
source: Intraflagellar cargoes interact with multiprotein complexes known as IFT particles that are organized into larger IFT trains as they enter the flagellum (Cole et al., 1998; Lechtreck et al., 2017; Pigino et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In most species, the IFT trains are transported anterogradely from the base to the tip of a flagellum by heterotrimeric kinesin-II.
source: In most species, the IFT trains are transported anterogradely from the base to the tip of a flagellum by heterotrimeric kinesin-II (Kozminski et al., 1995), but some species also use a second homodimeric kinesin to build more specialized sensory cilia (Snow et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Some species use a second homodimeric kinesin to build more specialized sensory cilia.
source: In most species, the IFT trains are transported anterogradely from the base to the tip of a flagellum by heterotrimeric kinesin-II (Kozminski et al., 1995), but some species also use a second homodimeric kinesin to build more specialized sensory cilia (Snow et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Once the trains reach the tip, they are reorganized and transported retrogradely to the ciliary base by dynein-1b.
source: Once the trains reach the tip, they are reorganized and transported retrogradely to the ciliary base by dynein-1b (Pazour et al., 1999; Porter et al., 1999; Signor et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Along the length of a cilium, the activities of kinesin and dynein motors are reciprocally coordinated, such that only one type of a motor is active at a time.
source: Along the length of a cilium, the activities of kinesin and dynein motors are reciprocally coordinated, such that only one type of a motor is active at a time (Shih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Trains move between the tip and base of the cilium without significant pauses or back-and-forth motion.
source: As a result, trains move between the tip and base of the cilium without significant pauses or back-and-forth motion (Dentler, 2005; Engel et al., 2009) and switch directions at the turnaround zones (Ishikawa and Marshall, 2011; Laib et al., 2009; Shih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Trains switch directions at the turnaround zones.
source: As a result, trains move between the tip and base of the cilium without significant pauses or back-and-forth motion (Dentler, 2005; Engel et al., 2009) and switch directions at the turnaround zones (Ishikawa and Marshall, 2011; Laib et al., 2009; Shih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dynein-1b requires kinesin-II activity to reach the ciliary tip.
source: Dynein-1b requires kinesin-II activity to reach the ciliary tip, suggesting that it travels on anterograde trains (Iomini et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2006; Rompolas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Retrograde traces of kinesin-II have not been frequently observed in Chlamydomonas.
source: Retrograde traces of kinesin-II have not been frequently observed in Chlamydomonas, and it remains unclear how kinesin-II returns to the basal body (Engel et al., 2009; Wingfield et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Anterograde and retrograde IFT trains have different sizes and depart at different frequencies.
source: Because anterograde and retrograde IFT trains have different sizes and depart at different frequencies (Dentler, 2005; Iomini et al., 2001), IFT trains must be remodeled at the distal tip and the flagellar base.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IFT trains must be remodeled at the distal tip and the flagellar base.
source: Because anterograde and retrograde IFT trains have different sizes and depart at different frequencies (Dentler, 2005; Iomini et al., 2001), IFT trains must be remodeled at the distal tip and the flagellar base.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited observations about train size and frequency differences.

claim: The mechanism underlying the remodeling of IFT complexes at the ciliary tip and base cannot be directly observed by conventional microscopy methods because multiple trains coexist in these turnaround zones.
source: The mechanism underlying the remodeling of IFT complexes at the ciliary tip and base cannot be directly observed by conventional microscopy methods because multiple trains coexist in these turnaround zones (Buisson et al., 2013; Iomini et al., 2001; Wren et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations supported by citations.

claim: The velocity of IFT27-GFP was 2.1 ± 0.4 µm s−1 in the anterograde direction.
source: The velocity of IFT27-GFP was 2.1 ± 0.4 µm s−1 in the anterograde direction and 3.0 ± 0.7 µm s−1 in the retrograde direction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, mean ± s.d., N = 80 trains in each direction).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: The velocity of IFT27-GFP was 3.0 ± 0.7 µm s−1 in the retrograde direction.
source: The velocity of IFT27-GFP was 2.1 ± 0.4 µm s−1 in the anterograde direction and 3.0 ± 0.7 µm s−1 in the retrograde direction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, mean ± s.d., N = 80 trains in each direction).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: On average, 2.4 retrograde trains were detected departing from the tip after the arrival of a single fluorescent anterograde train.
source: On average, 2.4 retrograde trains were detected departing from the tip after the arrival of a single fluorescent anterograde train (Figure 1f, N = 97), consistent with higher frequencies of retrograde IFT trains than anterograde IFT trains (Dentler, 2005; Iomini et al., 2001; Qin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: The number of retrograde trains per fluorescent anterograde train in PhotoGate assays (2.4) was significantly higher than the ratio of retrograde to anterograde train frequencies (1.15).
source: However, the number of retrograde trains per fluorescent anterograde train in PhotoGate assays (2.4, Figure 1c) was significantly higher (Welch's t-test, p=10−20) than the ratio of retrograde to anterograde train frequencies (1.15, Figure 1a) (Dentler, 2005; Iomini et al., 2001; Reck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: IFT complexes from different anterograde trains recombine with each other to form retrograde trains at the tip.
source: These observations suggested that IFT complexes from different anterograde trains recombine with each other to form retrograde trains at the tip.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PhotoGate experiments showing sub-proportional increase in retrograde trains.

claim: The fluorescent complexes in the anterograde trains disassemble and mix with a pool of 'dark' complexes from the other photobleached trains at the tip before they reorganize into retrograde trains.
source: Because the increase was sub-proportional with the number of anterograde trains, we concluded that the fluorescent complexes in the anterograde trains disassemble and mix with a pool of 'dark' complexes from the other photobleached trains at the tip before they reorganize into retrograde trains (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sub-proportional increase in retrograde trains observed in the experiments.

claim: The tip resting time of the first retrograde train was 3.1 ± 0.3 s.
source: When only a single fluorescent anterograde IFT27-GFP train was left unbleached near the base of the flagellum, the tip resting time of the first retrograde train was 3.1 ± 0.3 s (mean ± s.e.m., N = 97, Figure 2b), comparable to that of IFT cargos (Craft et al., 2015; Reck et al., 2016; Wren et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments.

claim: The tip resting time histogram of first retrograde trains fit well to a Gamma distribution with a shape parameter of 3 and a rate constant of ~1 s−1.
source: However, the tip resting time histogram of first retrograde trains fit well to a Gamma distribution with a shape parameter of 3 and a rate constant of ~1 s−1, indicating that tip turnaround of IFT trains occurs rapidly through a multistep process (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Tip turnaround of IFT trains occurs rapidly through a multistep process.
source: However, the tip resting time histogram of first retrograde trains fit well to a Gamma distribution with a shape parameter of 3 and a rate constant of ~1 s−1, indicating that tip turnaround of IFT trains occurs rapidly through a multistep process (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Gamma distribution fit to the data.

claim: The average time between successive retrograde trains (Δt) is 1.7 s.
source: We also observed that the tip resting time of first, second, third, and fourth fluorescent retrograde trains increases linearly (Figure 2c). Because the average time between successive retrograde trains (Δt = 1.7 s) is the same, we concluded that the tip departure is a purely stochastic process.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The tip departure is a purely stochastic process.
source: We also observed that the tip resting time of first, second, third, and fourth fluorescent retrograde trains increases linearly (Figure 2c). Because the average time between successive retrograde trains (Δt = 1.7 s) is the same, we concluded that the tip departure is a purely stochastic process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the linear increase in tip resting times with constant intervals.

claim: The linear fit to the tip resting times has a y-intercept of 1.3 s.
source: The linear fit to the tip resting times has a y-intercept of 1.3 s (Figure 2c), revealing that the departure of the first train takes longer than Δt.
evidence: This is a result from the linear fit analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The complexes dwell at the tip through another rate limiting process before they can depart from the tip.
source: The linear fit to the tip resting times has a y-intercept of 1.3 s (Figure 2c), revealing that the departure of the first train takes longer than Δt. Therefore, the complexes dwell at the tip through another rate limiting process before they can depart from the tip.
evidence: This is an inference based on the y-intercept being longer than the interval between successive trains.

claim: When extracellular calcium in media (0.34 mM) was chelated using 0.5 mM EGTA, the tip departure time increased to 2.8 s.
source: When extracellular calcium in media (0.34 mM) was chelated using 0.5 mM EGTA, the tip departure time increased to 2.8 s (Welch's t-test, p=0.01), whereas tip remodeling time (1.4 s) remained unaltered (Figure 2d,e).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the EGTA treatment experiments.

claim: Tip remodeling time (1.4 s) remained unaltered when extracellular calcium was chelated using 0.5 mM EGTA.
source: When extracellular calcium in media (0.34 mM) was chelated using 0.5 mM EGTA, the tip departure time increased to 2.8 s (Welch's t-test, p=0.01), whereas tip remodeling time (1.4 s) remained unaltered (Figure 2d,e).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the EGTA treatment experiments.

claim: Calcium has minimal effect on the breakdown of anterograde trains, but may have a regulatory role in the assembly or departure of retrograde trains.
source: Therefore, calcium has minimal effect on the breakdown of anterograde trains, but may have a regulatory role in the assembly or departure of retrograde trains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of EGTA on tip remodeling vs. departure times.

claim: Addition of 0.1 mM ciliobrevin D to media results in 50% reduction in the frequency of retrograde and anterograde trains.
source: Addition of 0.1 mM ciliobrevin D to media results in 50% reduction in the frequency of retrograde and anterograde trains, and 50% and 28% reduction in retrograde and anterograde train velocities, respectively (Shih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: The tip resting time of IFT27 increased over two-fold with ciliobrevin D treatment.
source: In this case, the tip resting time of IFT27 increased over two-fold (Figure 2e, p<10−4), suggesting that rapid turnover of IFT trains depends on dynein activity.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the ciliobrevin D treatment experiments.

claim: Rapid turnover of IFT trains depends on dynein activity.
source: In this case, the tip resting time of IFT27 increased over two-fold (Figure 2e, p<10−4), suggesting that rapid turnover of IFT trains depends on dynein activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the effect of the dynein inhibitor ciliobrevin D on tip resting time.

claim: D1bLIC moved continuously in the anterograde and retrograde directions at velocities similar to that of the IFT trains.
source: In the d1blic::D1bLIC-GFP strain, D1bLIC moved continuously in the anterograde and retrograde directions at velocities similar to that of the IFT trains (Reck et al., 2016) (Figure 3a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: KAP moved primarily in the anterograde direction to the flagellar tip at a similar speed to anterograde IFT27.
source: In the fla3::KAP-GFP strain, KAP moved primarily in the anterograde direction to the flagellar tip at a similar speed to anterograde IFT27 (Figure 3b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Retrograde traces of KAP were not frequently observed.
source: Unlike D1bLIC, retrograde traces of KAP were not frequently observed (Engel et al., 2009; Wingfield et al., 2017), suggesting that kinesin-II dissociates from IFT trains at the tip (Engel et al., 2009; Engel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments supported by citations.

claim: After arrival of a single anterograde D1bLIC-GFP train at the tip, on average 2.5 retrograde D1bLIC trains were detected.
source: After arrival of a single anterograde D1bLIC-GFP train at the tip, we detected on average 2.5 retrograde D1bLIC trains.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments.

claim: The average tip resting time until the departure of the first retrograde D1bLIC train was 1.8 ± 0.2 s.
source: The average tip resting time until the departure of the first retrograde train was 1.8 ± 0.2 s (mean ± s.e.m., N = 60, Figure 3d), with additional ~1.1 ± 0.1 s between subsequent departure events (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments.

claim: Single KAP-GFP trains moved anterogradely to the tip and rested at the tip for 2.2 ± 0.2 s.
source: PhotoGate imaging of KAP-GFP cells showed that single KAP-GFP trains moved anterogradely to the tip and rested at the tip for 2.2 ± 0.2 s (N = 95).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments.

claim: Individual KAP-GFP particles moved away from the tip by rapid saltatory motion.
source: Unlike D1bLIC, individual KAP-GFP particles moved away from the tip by rapid saltatory motion (Figure 3f,g, Figure 1—figure supplement 2c, Video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the PhotoGate experiments.

claim: KAP undergoes one-dimensional diffusion at 1.68 ± 0.04 µm2 s−1 within the flagellum after it departs from the tip.
source: Mean square displacement (MSD) analysis showed that KAP undergoes one-dimensional diffusion at 1.68 ± 0.04 µm2 s−1 (mean ± s.e.m., N = 27 traces) within the flagellum after it departs from the tip (Figure 3h), consistent with the values measured for tubulin and EB1 that undergo diffusion within the ciliary space (Craft et al., 2015; Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from MSD analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The tip resting time of KAP remained nearly constant at different steady-state flagellar lengths.
source: The tip resting time of KAP remained nearly constant at different steady-state flagellar lengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and was shorter than that of IFT27, indicating that departure of kinesin from the tip is independent of flagellar length and departure of retrograde trains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments at different flagellar lengths.

claim: Departure of kinesin from the tip is independent of flagellar length and departure of retrograde trains.
source: The tip resting time of KAP remained nearly constant at different steady-state flagellar lengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and was shorter than that of IFT27, indicating that departure of kinesin from the tip is independent of flagellar length and departure of retrograde trains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the constant tip resting time of KAP across different flagellar lengths.

claim: The majority (89%, N = 95) of KAP-GFPs simultaneously departed from the tip in a single step.
source: Unlike IFT trains, the majority (89%, N = 95) of KAP-GFPs simultaneously departed from the tip in a single step (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the PhotoGate experiments.

claim: Each anterograde train contains multiple (6) KAP-GFPs on average.
source: Because each anterograde train contains multiple (6) KAP-GFPs on average (Engel et al., 2009), this observation indicates that kinesin-II departs from the tip in the same oligomeric state as it arrives.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Kinesin-II departs from the tip in the same oligomeric state as it arrives.
source: Because each anterograde train contains multiple (6) KAP-GFPs on average (Engel et al., 2009), this observation indicates that kinesin-II departs from the tip in the same oligomeric state as it arrives.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that KAP-GFPs depart simultaneously despite multiple copies per train.

claim: After KAP detaches from the flagellar tip, it freely explores the space between the flagellar membrane and the axonemal surface rather than sliding along microtubules.
source: We concluded that after KAP detaches from the flagellar tip, it freely explores the space between the flagellar membrane and the axonemal surface rather than sliding along microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lateral fluctuation measurements during diffusion.

claim: Both tagged motors were expressed at near wild-type levels in the d1blic::D1bLIC-crCherry KAP-GFP strain.
source: Both tagged motors were expressed at near wild-type levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from Western blot analysis.

claim: Strong co-localization of D1bLIC-crCherry and KAP-GFP on anterograde trajectories was observed.
source: We observed strong co-localization of D1bLIC-crCherry and KAP-GFP on anterograde trajectories (Figure 4a), demonstrating that dynein-1b is carried to the flagellar tip by kinesin-II.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the two-color imaging experiments.

claim: Dynein-1b is carried to the flagellar tip by kinesin-II.
source: We observed strong co-localization of D1bLIC-crCherry and KAP-GFP on anterograde trajectories (Figure 4a), demonstrating that dynein-1b is carried to the flagellar tip by kinesin-II.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-localization observed in the two-color imaging experiments.

claim: Only D1bLIC-crCherry trains showed robust retrograde transport, while retrograde traces of KAP-GFP were rarely observed.
source: Only D1bLIC-crCherry trains showed robust retrograde transport, while retrograde traces of KAP-GFP were rarely observed, consistent with dissociation of kinesin-II from IFT trains at the tip.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the two-color imaging experiments.

claim: Kinesin-II and dynein-1b exit the flagellar tip independently from each other.
source: These results suggest that kinesin-II and dynein-1b exit the flagellar tip independently from each other.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the two-color PhotoGate experiments showing variable order of departure.

claim: The diffusion constant calculated from the fluorescence recovery (1.8 ± 0.1 μm2 s−1) was similar to the result of the MSD analysis.
source: The diffusion constant calculated from the fluorescence recovery (1.8 ± 0.1 μm2 s−1, Figure 5b) was similar to the result of the MSD analysis (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is a comparison of two independent measurements from different experimental approaches.

claim: The fluorescent background in KAP-GFP flagella increased towards the tip, suggesting a net efflux of diffusing KAP-GFP towards the cell body.
source: The fluorescent background in KAP-GFP flagella increased towards the tip, suggesting a net efflux of diffusing KAP-GFP towards the cell body (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments and an inference about the direction of net flux.

claim: During flagellar regrowth, the KAP-GFP gradient was maintained for all flagellar lengths.
source: During flagellar regrowth, the KAP-GFP gradient was maintained for all flagellar lengths (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the flagellar regrowth experiments.

claim: The influx of KAP-GFP fluorescence to the flagellum through anterograde IFT was statistically indistinguishable from the efflux of KAP-GFP to the base through one-dimensional diffusion in flagella.
source: The influx of KAP-GFP fluorescence to the flagellum through anterograde IFT was statistically indistinguishable from the efflux of KAP-GFP to the base through one-dimensional diffusion in flagella (Welch's t-test, p=0.80, N = 57, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of influx and efflux measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: KAP-GFP returns to the cell body by diffusing from the flagellar tip.
source: These results strongly indicate that KAP-GFP returns to the cell body by diffusing from the flagellar tip.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRAP experiments and flux measurements.

claim: The total amount of KAP localized to the base and flagellum increased by two-fold with flagellar length.
source: The total amount of KAP localized to the base and flagellum increased by two-fold with flagellar length, indicating the upregulation of IFT components during flagellar growth.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the confocal microscopy experiments during flagellar regrowth.

claim: IFT components are upregulated during flagellar growth.
source: The total amount of KAP localized to the base and flagellum increased by two-fold with flagellar length, indicating the upregulation of IFT components during flagellar growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the increase in total KAP fluorescence during flagellar regrowth.

claim: The fluorescence intensity at the flagellar base was highest for short flagella (1–4 µm) and decreased ~4 fold as cells grew full-length flagella (~10 µm).
source: The fluorescence intensity at the flagellar base was highest for short flagella (1–4 µm) and decreased ~4 fold as cells grew full-length flagella (~10 µm, Figure 6b), significantly larger than ~1.6 fold reduction reported previously (Ludington et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the confocal microscopy experiments during flagellar regrowth.

claim: The KAP fluorescence in the flagellum was low in short flagella and increased ~10 fold as the flagellar length reached the steady-state.
source: We also observed that the KAP fluorescence in the flagellum was low in short flagella and increased ~10 fold as the flagellar length reached the steady-state (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the confocal microscopy experiments during flagellar regrowth.

claim: Unlike KAP-GFP, basal body fluorescence of IFT20-GFP remained nearly constant across all flagellar lengths.
source: Unlike KAP-GFP, basal body fluorescence of IFT20-GFP remained nearly constant across all flagellar lengths in IFT20::IFT20-GFP cells (Figure 6c), presumably because they are rapidly returned to the base through active transport.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the confocal microscopy experiments during flagellar regrowth.

claim: IFT20-GFP is rapidly returned to the base through active transport.
source: Unlike KAP-GFP, basal body fluorescence of IFT20-GFP remained nearly constant across all flagellar lengths in IFT20::IFT20-GFP cells (Figure 6c), presumably because they are rapidly returned to the base through active transport.
evidence: This is an inference based on the constant basal body fluorescence of IFT20-GFP.

claim: Chlamydomonas grows ~1.5X longer flagella in the presence of Li+.
source: Chlamydomonas grows ~1.5X longer flagella in the presence of Li+ (Nakamura et al., 1987) by recruiting flagellar proteins from the cell body pool into the flagella (Nakamura et al., 1987) rather than requiring new protein synthesis (Wilson and Lefebvre, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: KAP gets depleted at the basal body at equilibrium in Li+ treated cells.
source: In agreement with our model, we observed that KAP gets depleted at the basal body at equilibrium.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Li+ treatment experiments.

claim: The KAP fluorescence localized to a flagellum correlated strongly with flagellar length (Pearson's R = 0.86) in Li+ treated cells.
source: The KAP fluorescence localized to a flagellum correlated strongly with flagellar length (Pearson's R = 0.86), similar to untreated cells.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the Li+ treatment experimental data.

claim: In the absence of new protein synthesis, Chlamydomonas can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation.
source: In the absence of new protein synthesis, Chlamydomonas can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation, suggesting that the cytoplasmic pool of flagellar proteins is at least one half of that localized to the flagellar compartment (Rosenbaum et al., 1969).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The cytoplasmic pool of flagellar proteins is at least one half of that localized to the flagellar compartment.
source: In the absence of new protein synthesis, Chlamydomonas can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation, suggesting that the cytoplasmic pool of flagellar proteins is at least one half of that localized to the flagellar compartment (Rosenbaum et al., 1969).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that half-length flagella can be grown without new protein synthesis.

claim: Over a wide range of flagellar lengths (2–22 µm), KAP gets depleted at the basal body when the flagella reach their equilibrium length.
source: Therefore, over a wide range of flagellar lengths (2–22 µm), KAP gets depleted at the basal body when the flagella reach their equilibrium length.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiments with control, Li+ treated, and cycloheximide treated cells.

claim: Disassembly of anterograde trains and reassembly of the retrograde trains is a multistep process regulated by extracellular calcium and the concentration of active dynein motors.
source: Kinetic analysis of the tip resting time revealed that disassembly of anterograde trains and reassembly of the retrograde trains is a multistep process regulated by extracellular calcium and the concentration of active dynein motors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Gamma distribution fit and the effects of EGTA and ciliobrevin D treatments.

claim: Kinesin-II drives anterograde trains in a highly processive fashion and then dissociates from the IFT trains when they reach at the flagellar tip.
source: Kinesin-II drives anterograde trains in a highly processive fashion and then dissociates from the IFT trains when they reach at the flagellar tip.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PhotoGate experiments tracking KAP-GFP.

claim: KAP-GFP returns to the flagellar base by diffusing within the flagellum, similar to the diffusion of kinesin-1 in mammalian neurons.
source: KAP-GFP then returns to the flagellar base by diffusing within the flagellum, similar to the diffusion of kinesin-1 in mammalian neurons (Blasius et al., 2013) and in contrast to the retrograde transport of kinesin-II observed in other cilia (Signor et al., 1999; Broekhuis et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2014; Prevo et al., 2015), see below).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRAP and MSD experiments, with comparison to other systems via citations.

claim: The diffusion of KAP-GFP represents the movement of the entire heterotrimeric kinesin-II complex.
source: We propose that the diffusion of KAP-GFP represents the movement of the entire heterotrimeric kinesin-II complex because KAP and the kinesin-II motor subunits co-sediment in sucrose density gradients of purified flagella extracts (Cole et al., 1998; Mueller et al., 2005) and neither KAP nor FLA10 accumulate in flagella during inactivation of retrograde transport (Engel et al., 2012; Pedersen et al., 2006; Reck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a proposal based on cited biochemical evidence and observations from mutant studies.

claim: Dynein-1b is carried as an inactive motor complex on anterograde trains.
source: Because kinesin and dynein motors do not compete against each other in a tug-of-war on anterograde trains (Shih et al., 2013), we concluded that dynein-1b is carried as an inactive motor complex (Toropova et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017), and it actively engages with microtubules only when it reaches the flagellar tip (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of tug-of-war and supported by citations about inactive dynein states.

claim: Dynein-1b actively engages with microtubules only when it reaches the flagellar tip.
source: Because kinesin and dynein motors do not compete against each other in a tug-of-war on anterograde trains (Shih et al., 2013), we concluded that dynein-1b is carried as an inactive motor complex (Toropova et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017), and it actively engages with microtubules only when it reaches the flagellar tip (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that dynein-1b only shows retrograde movement after reaching the tip.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, the axoneme contains nine doublet microtubules, each composed of a complete A-tubule (with 13 protofilaments) and an incomplete B-tubule (with 10 protofilaments).
source: In Chlamydomonas, the axoneme contains nine doublet microtubules, each composed of a complete A-tubule (with 13 protofilaments) and an incomplete B-tubule (with 10 protofilaments).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Chlamydomonas axoneme structure.

claim: The B-tubule terminates before the A-tubule less than 1 µm from the flagellar tip.
source: The B-tubule terminates before the A-tubule less than 1 µm from the flagellar tip (Ringo, 1967; Satish Tammana et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Anterograde IFT trains are transported primarily on the B-tubule, whereas retrograde IFT trains are transported on the A-tubule.
source: Recent electron microscopy studies have revealed that anterograde IFT trains are transported primarily on the B-tubule, whereas retrograde IFT trains are transported on the A-tubule (Stepanek and Pigino, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited electron microscopy study.

claim: The pausing of IFT particles observed at the flagellar tip in Chlamydomonas may reflect the time involved in the re-organization of the IFT particles and the time required for switching between microtubule tracks.
source: The pausing of IFT particles observed at the flagellar tip in Chlamydomonas may therefore reflect not only the time involved in the re-organization of the IFT particles, but also the time required for switching between microtubule tracks.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the knowledge of microtubule track organization.

claim: In C. elegans, heterotrimeric kinesin-II is concentrated near the basal body region and transports anterograde IFT particles into the proximal doublet segment, where they are gradually handed over to a homodimeric kinesin-II, OSM-3, for transport into the distal singlet segment.
source: In C. elegans, heterotrimeric kinesin-II is concentrated near the basal body region and transports anterograde IFT particles into the proximal doublet segment, where they are gradually handed over to a homodimeric kinesin-II, OSM-3, for transport into the distal singlet segment (Prevo et al., 2015; Snow et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans IFT supported by citations.

claim: In C. elegans and other metazoan cilia, both the heterotrimeric and homodimeric kinesin-II motors are recycled to the ciliary base by retrograde IFT, not by diffusion.
source: Unlike Chlamydomonas, both the heterotrimeric and homodimeric kinesin-II motors are recycled to the ciliary base by retrograde IFT, not by diffusion, in these and other metazoan cilia studied to date (Broekhuis et al., 2014; Mijalkovic et al., 2017; Prevo et al., 2015; Signor et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about metazoan cilia supported by citations.

claim: IFT particles and motors move processively in the Chlamydomonas flagellum, with little or no evidence for the frequent pausing and reversal along the axoneme previously described in C. elegans or mouse olfactory sensory cilia.
source: IFT particles and motors move processively in the Chlamydomonas flagellum (Dentler, 2005), with little or no evidence for the frequent pausing and reversal along the axoneme previously described in C. elegans or mouse olfactory sensory cilia (Mijalkovic et al., 2017; Prevo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of observations in Chlamydomonas with cited observations in other organisms.

claim: Acceleration and deceleration of IFT motors near turnaround zones was not observed in Chlamydomonas.
source: We also did not observe acceleration and deceleration of IFT motors near turnaround zones, nor the instantaneous (<600 ms) reversal of dynein-1b at the ciliary tip described in C. elegans (Mijalkovic et al., 2017; Prevo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about what was not observed in the experiments, contrasted with cited observations in C. elegans.

claim: Both the frequency and speed of IFT is higher in Chlamydomonas than that measured in metazoan cilia.
source: In addition, both the frequency and speed of IFT is higher in Chlamydomonas (Dentler, 2005; Engel et al., 2009; Engel et al., 2012; Iomini et al., 2001; Reck et al., 2016; Snow et al., 2004; Williams et al., 2014; Wingfield et al., 2017) than that measured thus far in metazoan cilia (Li et al., 2015; Yi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of measurements in Chlamydomonas with measurements in metazoan cilia, both supported by citations.

claim: According to the balance point model, flagellar length is set when flagellar assembly and disassembly rates reach equilibrium.
source: According to the balance point model, flagellar length is set when flagellar assembly and disassembly rates reach equilibrium (Marshall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the balance point model supported by a citation.

claim: The disassembly rate is independent of flagellar length.
source: While the disassembly rate is independent of flagellar length (Kozminski et al., 1995), the assembly rate is determined by the injection of IFT trains (Marshall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The assembly rate is determined by the injection of IFT trains.
source: While the disassembly rate is independent of flagellar length (Kozminski et al., 1995), the assembly rate is determined by the injection of IFT trains (Marshall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The amount of material being transported by IFT trains to the tip is correlated strongly with the amount of material localized to the flagellar base.
source: The amount of material being transported by these trains to the tip is correlated strongly with the amount of material localized to the flagellar base (Ludington et al., 2013; Ludington et al., 2015; Wren et al., 2013), which serves as a loading dock.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IFT train size and the number of ciliary cargos per train scales inversely with flagellar length.
source: Previous studies showed that IFT train size and the number of ciliary cargos per train scales inversely with flagellar length (Craft et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2009), consistent with the reduction of the assembly rate as flagella elongate (Marshall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Diffusion leads to a large accumulation of kinesin-II in the flagellum as the flagellum grows longer, while the amount of kinesin-II at the base decreases several-fold.
source: Our results show that the majority of kinesin-II dissociates from IFT trains at the flagellar tip and diffuses within the flagellum. Diffusion leads to a large accumulation of kinesin-II in the flagellum as the flagellum grows longer, while the amount of kinesin-II at the base decreases several-fold.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the confocal microscopy measurements during flagellar regrowth.

claim: Lower amounts of kinesin-II are available to bring new anterograde IFT trains to the flagellar tip as flagella elongate.
source: As a result, lower amounts of kinesin-II are available to bring new anterograde IFT trains to the flagellar tip.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the depletion of kinesin-II at the basal body as flagella elongate.

claim: Depletion of kinesin-II at the basal body may lead to a reduction in the IFT train size and the rate of flagellar assembly as the flagella elongate.
source: This may lead to a reduction in the IFT train size and the rate of flagellar assembly as the flagella elongate (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: This is a speculation about the consequences of kinesin-II depletion.

claim: A recent theoretical study demonstrated that increased diffusion time of kinesin-II in longer flagella can explain the inverse relationship between length and IFT motor recruitment rate.
source: Indeed, a recent theoretical study demonstrated that increased diffusion time of kinesin-II in longer flagella can explain the inverse relationship between length and IFT motor recruitment rate (Hendel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited theoretical study that supports the authors' model.

claim: KAP intensity at the basal body correlates with KAP loading on IFT trains and the assembly rate during flagellar regeneration.
source: Consistent with this model, previous studies showed that KAP intensity at the basal body correlates with KAP loading on IFT trains and the assembly rate during flagellar regeneration (Ludington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study that supports the authors' model.

claim: In the temperature-sensitive mutant strain fla10ts, inactivation of kinesin-II motility ceases IFT and leads to resorption of the flagellum at a constant rate.
source: In the temperature-sensitive mutant strain fla10ts, inactivation of kinesin-II motility ceases IFT and leads to resorption of the flagellum at a constant rate (Kozminski et al., 1995; Marshall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: At intermediate temperatures, flagellar length correlates strongly with the estimated fraction of active kinesin-II motors in fla10ts cells.
source: At intermediate temperatures, flagellar length correlates strongly with the estimated fraction of active kinesin-II motors in fla10ts cells (Marshall and Rosenbaum, 2001), indicating that the amount of active kinesin-II limits flagellar growth.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: The amount of active kinesin-II limits flagellar growth.
source: At intermediate temperatures, flagellar length correlates strongly with the estimated fraction of active kinesin-II motors in fla10ts cells (Marshall and Rosenbaum, 2001), indicating that the amount of active kinesin-II limits flagellar growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion from a cited study that supports the authors' model.

claim: Altering the amount of KAP available for the flagellar compartment positively correlates with the flagellar length.
source: The experiments performed under Li+ and cycloheximide treatments (Figure 6d) also support the idea that altering the amount of KAP available for the flagellar compartment positively correlates with the flagellar length and that the equilibrium length is set when KAP gets depleted below a certain threshold at the basal body.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Li+ and cycloheximide treatment experiments.

claim: The equilibrium length is set when KAP gets depleted below a certain threshold at the basal body.
source: The experiments performed under Li+ and cycloheximide treatments (Figure 6d) also support the idea that altering the amount of KAP available for the flagellar compartment positively correlates with the flagellar length and that the equilibrium length is set when KAP gets depleted below a certain threshold at the basal body.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Li+ and cycloheximide treatment experiments.

claim: IFT components are rapidly recycled to the cell body by dynein-1b.
source: Unlike kinesin-II, IFT components are rapidly recycled to the cell body by dynein-1b and the amount of these components at the flagellar base remains nearly constant as the flagella elongate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the IFT20-GFP measurements during flagellar regrowth.

claim: The amount of IFT components at the flagellar base remains nearly constant as the flagella elongate.
source: Unlike kinesin-II, IFT components are rapidly recycled to the cell body by dynein-1b and the amount of these components at the flagellar base remains nearly constant as the flagella elongate.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the IFT20-GFP measurements during flagellar regrowth.

claim: The abundance of IFT components and dynein-1b at the flagellar base is not limiting to maintain the length.
source: Therefore, the abundance of IFT components and dynein-1b at the flagellar base is not limiting to maintain the length, consistent with previous observations that a small amount of IFT complexes and dynein-1b is sufficient to maintain fully grown flagella (Reck et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the constant basal body levels of IFT components and supported by citations.

claim: Diffusion is proposed to play a role in setting the length of bacterial flagella.
source: Diffusion is also proposed to play a role in setting the length of bacterial flagella (Renault et al., 2017), long polymers made from a single protein flagellin.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: In bacterial flagella, flagellins are injected into the channel of the filament and they diffuse to reach the assembly site at the filament tip, generating a concentration gradient decreasing towards the tip.
source: Similar to the flagellar length control model originally proposed for Chlamydomonas (Levy, 1974), flagellins are injected into the channel of the filament and they diffuse to reach the assembly site at the filament tip, generating a concentration gradient decreasing towards the tip.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial flagella supported by citations.

claim: As the bacterial filament elongates, it grows more slowly because it takes longer for the components to reach the tip.
source: As the filament elongates, it grows more slowly because it takes longer for the components to reach the tip.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial flagellar growth.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, diffusion of kinesin-II from the tip sets a concentration gradient decreasing towards the basal body.
source: In contrast to bacterial flagellin, structural components are carried to the tip by IFT in eukaryotic flagella. In Chlamydomonas, we showed that diffusion of kinesin-II from the tip sets a concentration gradient decreasing towards the basal body, and its return to the flagellar base is delayed as the flagella elongate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRAP and confocal microscopy experiments.

claim: Return of kinesin-II to the flagellar base is delayed as the flagella elongate.
source: In contrast to bacterial flagellin, structural components are carried to the tip by IFT in eukaryotic flagella. In Chlamydomonas, we showed that diffusion of kinesin-II from the tip sets a concentration gradient decreasing towards the basal body, and its return to the flagellar base is delayed as the flagella elongate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diffusion measurements and modeling.

claim: The delay in kinesin-II return limits the amount of kinesin-II available for building longer flagella.
source: This delay limits the amount of kinesin-II available for building longer flagella.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the depletion of kinesin-II at the basal body as flagella elongate.

claim: The kinesin-II mutant strains fla10ts and fla3 maintain nearly full-length flagella at permissive temperatures although they accumulate significantly lower amounts of kinesin-II in the flagellar compartment.
source: Our model is challenged by studies showing that the kinesin-II mutant strains fla10ts and fla3 maintain nearly full-length flagella at permissive temperatures although they accumulate significantly lower amounts of kinesin-II in the flagellar compartment (Kozminski et al., 1995; Mueller et al., 2005; Pedersen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies that challenges the authors' model.

claim: fla3 cells exhibit slower flagellar regeneration.
source: Remarkably, fla3 cells exhibit slower flagellar regeneration (Mueller et al., 2005), consistent with our prediction that the lower amount of kinesin-II negatively affects the assembly rate.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study that supports the authors' model.

claim: A more recent study showed that fla10ts flagella contain wild-type levels of kinesin-II at permissive temperatures.
source: However, a more recent study showed that fla10ts flagella contain wild-type levels of kinesin-II at permissive temperatures (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study that contradicts earlier findings.

claim: Flagella that contain lower amounts of kinesin-II can still maintain nearly full-length if they also have a lower disassembly rate.
source: According to the balance-point model, flagella that contain lower amounts of kinesin-II can still maintain nearly full-length if they also have a lower disassembly rate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the balance-point model.

claim: IFT is required for efficiently removing certain axonemal precursors.
source: This could negatively affect the disassembly rate because IFT is required for efficiently removing certain axonemal precursors (Qin et al., 2004) and resorbing the flagellum prior to mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Flagellar resorption before mitosis occurs at a faster rate than flagellar disassembly after inactivation of IFT.
source: Indeed, flagellar resorption before mitosis occurs at a faster rate than flagellar disassembly after inactivation of IFT (Marshall et al., 2005; Pan and Snell, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: IFT components are upregulated and accumulate in large numbers at the flagellar base after deflagellation.
source: Several studies have shown that IFT components are upregulated and accumulate in large numbers at the flagellar base after deflagellation (Albee et al., 2013; Lefebvre and Rosenbaum, 1986; Stolc et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: A large pool of IFT components in the cytoplasm partially exchanges with the flagellar pool.
source: Additionally, a large pool of IFT components in the cytoplasm partially exchanges with the flagellar pool (Buisson et al., 2013; Engel et al., 2009; Wingfield et al., 2017) because cells can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation under complete inhibition of protein synthesis (Rosenbaum et al., 1969).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Cells can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation under complete inhibition of protein synthesis.
source: Additionally, a large pool of IFT components in the cytoplasm partially exchanges with the flagellar pool (Buisson et al., 2013; Engel et al., 2009; Wingfield et al., 2017) because cells can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation under complete inhibition of protein synthesis (Rosenbaum et al., 1969).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.
